newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Turkish minister in Libya ahead of Erbakan visit.
newsitem.headline: Turkish minister in Libya ahead of Erbakan visit.

text.p: Turkey's energy minister has started talks with Libyan officials ahead of a controversial visit this week by Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.

Recai Kutan on Wednesday night co-chaired with Maatouq Mohamed Maatouq, Libyan Minister of Education, Youth and Sports, Scientific Research and Training, a meeting which discussed cooperation between the two countries, said the official Libyan news agency JANA, received in Tunis.

"We hope to reach positive results able to boost bilateral cooperation in the economic, trade, industry and technical fields between the two countries," JANA quoted Kutan as saying at the opening session.
JANA later said Kutan also discussed with Libyan Energy Minister Abdullah Salem al-Badri ways to boost cooperation in the energy and oil fields.

On his arrival in Tripoli on Wednesday, Kutan said Erbakan, expected in Libya on Friday, would lead a senior delegation including businessmen and representatives from all political parties. He also renewed Turkey's call for an end to U.N. sanctions against Libya.
Erbakan on Wednesday was in Egypt as part of a trip that includes Libya, the target of limited U.N. sanctions, renewing concern at home and abroad he wants to change Turkey's pro-Western stance.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, the Islamists' conservative coalition partner, described the visits as ill-timed and a member of her wing of the government threatened to resign over the trip.
Washington, already wary of modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, has expressed its own disquiet.
Turkish officials want Libya to repay debts of up to $365 million due to Turkish contractors.

Maatouq said during his discussions with Kutan that Libya was seeking joint ventures with Turkish firms and for a reinforcement of industrial cooperation, joint investments, and an expansion of bilateral trade.

Few foreign leaders have visited Tripoli since the United Nations imposed an air and limited trade embargo on Libya in 1991 for its refusal to hand over two Libyans suspected of blowing up a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988.
Libya dismissed U.S. criticism of Erbakan's visit. The foreign ministry denounced what it called U.S. "threats and warnings".
